prompt: I'm a product manager at Pinnacle, a field-service platform. Over the last 3 months, 12 of our enterprise sales calls have included prospects asking whether our mobile app works offline. Our current app requires constant connectivity. Last week, a prospect representing 450 field technicians told us they chose a competitor specifically because we lack offline capability. My assumption is that most of these requests come from companies operating in rural areas with poor coverage, but I don't actually know if that's true or if the need is broader. The open question is how many of our existing 2,300 customers would actually use offline mode regularly versus how many prospects just want it as a safety net. I need a clear recommendation on whether to prioritize offline mode in our Q3 roadmap or deprioritize it, with reasoning I can present to our VP of Product. What should I ask or investigate to make this call?

I run subscription billing at Northwind Analytics. In the past 60 days, annual plan cancellations jumped 34% compared to the previous 6-month average. We noticed the spike started right after our March 14 price increase for new customers, though existing annual subscribers were grandfathered. My assumption is that the cancellations are driven by customers seeing the new prices on our pricing page and preemptively canceling before their renewal, but I haven't confirmed this. The unknown is whether these customers are churning because of perceived value or because they're actually switching to a competitor offering lower prices. I want a structured analysis of what evidence I should gather next and whether a pricing adjustment is warranted now or if I should wait for more data. I need to present this to our CFO and head of sales by April 28.

I'm the lead PM at BrightPath, an employee-learning platform. We have 4 weeks of engineering capacity before our next release freeze. We ran two small onboarding tests last quarter: Test A used a guided walkthrough with progress indicators, and Test B used a single interactive demo that let users explore freely. Test A had 18% completion of onboarding with 312 participants. Test B had 22% completion with 298 participants, but users in Test B took 40% longer to reach their first course. My assumption is that Test B's higher completion rate means it's the better path, but I'm unsure if the longer time to first course will hurt retention. The open question is whether completion or speed-to-value matters more for our 30-day activation metric. I need a recommendation on which experiment to scale and what additional data would make the decision clearer, to share with our engineering lead and growth team.

I'm a product manager at Clearwater, a B2B expense management tool. Our largest client, Meridian Corp with 1,200 seats, requested a custom reporting dashboard last October. We built a basic version that launched January 15, but as of March 30, only 3 out of 47 Meridian users have logged into the reporting section more than once. Now two other enterprise prospects are asking about advanced reporting capabilities, and our sales team thinks it could be a differentiator. My assumption is that the low usage at Meridian means the current reports don't answer the right questions, but I don't know what specific reports or data those prospects actually need. The open question is whether there's genuine demand for reporting across our customer base or if this is just a checkbox feature that prospects ask about but never use. I need a plan for what discovery activities to run before committing engineering resources, to present to our product director.

I'm the head of product at Solstice, a project management tool for creative teams. We just analyzed our Q1 satisfaction survey with 1,840 responses. Our overall score is 72 out of 100, but users at companies with fewer than 50 employees rated us 89 out of 100, while users at companies over 500 employees rated us 61. We have 3,200 customers total, and roughly 70% of revenue comes from the enterprise segment. My assumption is that smaller teams find our tool intuitive because they have simpler workflows, but I'm not sure if the enterprise dissatisfaction is about missing features or about implementation and training gaps. The unknown is whether improving satisfaction for enterprise users would require fundamentally different functionality or just better support and onboarding. I need guidance on how to interpret this split and what to investigate next, so I can build a case for our Q3 investment priorities to share with the executive team.

I'm a product manager at Redwood, a marketing automation platform. We still support an integration with Cresta CRM that we built in 2018. As of April 2024, only 14 of our 8,500 accounts actively use it, and those 14 accounts generate $210,000 in annual revenue. Maintaining the integration costs us roughly 3 engineering sprints per year due to API changes on Cresta's side. My assumption is that most of those 14 accounts are legacy customers who haven't migrated to newer CRMs, but I don't know if switching would cause them significant business disruption or if they'd churn. The open question is whether the revenue from those accounts justifies the ongoing maintenance cost and opportunity cost of not using those sprints elsewhere. I need a framework for making this sunset decision and a recommendation on next steps, which I'll present to our VP of Engineering and Customer Success director.

I'm the founder of Waypoint, a team-scheduling app. Over the past 90 days, we lost 68 customers, and I conducted churn interviews with 22 of them between February and March. The top themes: 14 mentioned they found a cheaper alternative, 8 said their team stopped using the app after the first month, and 5 complained about lack of calendar sync. Interviews were semi-structured, so I didn't ask everyone the same questions. My assumption is that the calendar sync issue is the most actionable problem since price sensitivity is hard to address and low engagement might be a symptom rather than a cause. The unknown is whether fixing calendar sync would actually retain those customers or if the cheaper alternatives would still win. I need help turning these notes into a discovery plan for next quarter that tells me what to validate before building anything, to share with my co-founder and our one product designer.

I'm a product manager at Lumen, a design-collaboration tool. We're considering a paid add-on that provides advanced version history with branching and comparison views. No customer has requested this explicitly, but 3 of our top 10 accounts mentioned during renewal calls in January that they struggle with tracking design iterations. Our basic version history is free and included in all plans. My assumption is that power users at larger companies would pay $15 per seat per month for advanced version control, but I have no evidence of willingness to pay. The open question is whether customers would see this as a valuable upgrade or an annoying paywall for something they expect to be included. I need a plan for testing demand before we commit any engineering time, which I'll present to our head of product and finance lead. What should I do to validate interest and pricing without building the feature first?

I'm the growth PM at Aurora, an e-commerce platform. We ran a two-week test comparing our current 3-page checkout against a new single-page design. The current checkout had 1,240 sessions with 62 completed purchases. The new single-page checkout had 1,180 sessions with 55 completed purchases. The difference isn't statistically significant, but the single-page design had a 28% higher add-to-cart rate before the final confirmation step. My assumption is that the single-page design reduces friction early but creates hesitation at the final commit, possibly due to less review time. The unknown is whether the higher add-to-cart rate would translate to more purchases with a larger sample or if the design fundamentally breaks trust at the final step. I need a recommendation on which design to move forward with and what additional test would give us clearer signal, to present to our CTO and head of marketing.

I'm the product lead at Bazaar, a new marketplace connecting freelance chefs with people hosting private dinner parties. We launched 6 months ago and have 340 hosts and 90 chefs signed up, but only 47 bookings completed. I've identified 8 assumptions we haven't validated: hosts will pay a 15% booking fee, chefs want this type of gig, hosts care more about cuisine type than price, repeat bookings will drive growth, chefs will set their own menus, hosts will book 2+ weeks in advance, quality photos drive bookings, and weekday demand exists. My assumption is that the booking fee tolerance is the riskiest assumption since hosts already pay for ingredients and venue, but I'm not sure. The unknown is which assumption, if wrong, would collapse the entire business model. I need help figuring out which assumption to test first and how, so I can present a prioritized testing roadmap to our investors at the June 15 board meeting.

I'm a product manager at BrightPath, a project management tool for marketing teams. Last week, our main competitor TaskHive launched an AI-powered content calendar feature that auto-suggests posting times based on audience activity. Since then, three of our 200 customers have mentioned it in support chats, and one asked if we have something similar on our roadmap. Our current Q3 plan focuses on reporting improvements that 45 customers requested in our last survey. I'm assuming that these three mentions represent casual curiosity rather than purchase-decision pressure, but I'm not sure what threshold of customer mentions should actually trigger a roadmap change. Should we reprioritize to add a content calendar feature, or stay the course with reporting? I need a recommendation on whether the competitor launch should change our roadmap priorities, for me to present to our leadership team next Thursday.

I'm the founder of NoteStream, a collaborative note-taking web app for research teams. Looking at our analytics from January through March 2024, 38% of our 12,000 monthly web sessions come from phones, but our mobile web experience is clunky—users on mobile have a 22% lower completion rate for creating notes compared to desktop. We have a team of six engineers. Building a native mobile app would take at least three months based on our current velocity. I'm assuming that the 38% mobile session rate indicates real demand for a native app rather than just casual browsing, but I don't know whether those mobile users would actually download and use an app versus just wanting a better mobile web experience. I need your analysis on whether we should build a native mobile app or improve mobile web, for me to share with my co-founder and engineering lead at our planning meeting.

I'm a product manager at DataPulse, an analytics platform for small businesses. On March 1, 2024, we reduced our free-tier query limit from 500 to 200 per month, hoping to convert more users to paid plans. It's now March 15, and our activation rate—the percentage of signups who run at least five queries in their first week—dropped from 34% to 28%. We've had 420 new signups since the change. My assumption is that the limit reduction directly caused the activation drop by frustrating new users before they could experience value. But I'm uncertain whether two weeks of data is enough to conclude this is a sustained problem versus a short-term adjustment, or whether other factors like our concurrent landing page redesign could be contributing. I need a recommendation on whether to revert the free-tier limit change, for me to present to our growth team on Friday.

I'm the product lead at CodeForge, a code review tool for small engineering teams. We currently have 87 active users across 12 companies. We want to understand why only 30% of teams that start a trial convert to paid after 14 days. The challenge is our user base is so small that I worry about interview fatigue—if we talk to too many people, we'll have no one left to validate potential solutions later. My assumption is that the low conversion stems from unclear value perception during the trial rather than product gaps, but I'm not sure how to select which users to interview when our pool is this limited without biasing our findings toward the most vocal or available respondents. I need a plan for who to interview and how many, for me to review with my team before we start scheduling conversations next week.

I'm a product manager at ShopEase, an e-commerce platform for independent retailers. Over the past six months, we've received localization requests from 14 potential customers: 8 from Germany, 4 from Japan, and 2 from Brazil. Our product is currently English-only. We have 1,200 active customers, all in English-speaking markets. Translating the app and adding multi-currency support would cost approximately $90,000 and take our three-person front-end team about four months. My assumption is that these 14 requests represent the tip of demand in those markets rather than the total addressable interest, but I genuinely don't know whether entering non-English markets will generate enough revenue to justify the investment, or whether we'd be better off deepening our English-market features instead. I need a recommendation on whether to invest in localization now, for me to present to our CEO and finance lead at our quarterly planning session.

I'm the product manager at FlowBoard, a workflow automation tool. Looking at our monthly cohort retention data, I noticed something unusual. Our February 2024 cohort of 340 users flattens at 22% day-60 retention, while every other cohort from the past year flattens around 38-42%. Nothing obvious changed in February—same acquisition channels, same onboarding flow, same pricing. The only difference I can spot is that we had a 15% spike in signups from a product launch on February 8 that brought in users who might have different characteristics. My assumption is that those launch-driven users have lower intent than our typical organic signups, which would explain the retention drop. But I'm unsure whether this cohort anomaly indicates a real problem with our product that emerged in February, or if it's purely an acquisition source quality issue that will resolve as that cohort churns out. I need your interpretation of what this retention pattern means and whether we should take action, for me to share with our growth team on Monday.

I'm the founder of SecureVault, a new compliance management tool for mid-size companies. We have five pilot customers who signed up between January and March 2024, paying $800 per month each. Four of the five were sold through my personal network and required extensive hand-holding during setup, averaging 12 hours of my time per customer. One customer self-served through our website with minimal support. We're now deciding how to scale. Going sales-led would mean hiring account executives and potentially growing revenue faster per customer, while self-serve would require more product investment in onboarding but could scale to more customers with lower acquisition costs. My assumption is that our target market of companies with 50-500 employees typically expects a sales relationship for tools at this price point, but I'm uncertain whether that expectation is changing, or whether our one self-serve customer is an outlier or a signal of what's possible. I need a recommendation on whether to pursue a self-serve or sales-led model, for me to present to my co-founder and our advisor at our strategy session next week.

I'm a product manager at TeamSync, a collaboration platform for remote teams. One customer, Meridian Corp, has been very vocal in our feedback forum and on three sales calls about needing granular admin permissions—they want to restrict certain team members from deleting channels or inviting external guests. No other customer has requested this in the 18 months since launch. We have 340 active team accounts. Building this feature would take our two backend engineers approximately six weeks based on similar past work. My assumption is that Meridian is an outlier with unusually strict compliance requirements, and that most teams are fine with the current binary admin/member roles. But I'm not sure whether Meridian's request signals a need that many customers have but haven't articulated, especially as we target larger enterprise accounts. I need your assessment of whether this is a real widespread need or just one loud customer, for me to present to our product and engineering leads at our prioritization meeting on Thursday.

I'm the product lead at MeetBrief, a meeting productivity tool for distributed teams. Several customers have asked if we can automatically generate AI summaries of their meetings. We currently have 2,800 active users on our $15/month plan. Building this feature would require significant investment—we'd need to integrate with recording APIs, process audio, and generate summaries, which we estimate would take our four-person engineering team about two months and add $4,000 monthly in compute costs. My assumption is that teams who have long recurring meetings would find enough value in summaries to justify a price increase, but I don't know whether customers would actually pay more for this feature or if they see it as something that should be included in their current plan. I need a recommendation on how to test whether teams will pay for an AI summary feature before we commit engineering time, for me to discuss with our CEO and engineering lead at our product review next Wednesday.

I'm a product manager at GreenLeaf, a sustainability reporting platform for mid-size companies. Our team of four engineers can realistically complete about 24 story points per two-week sprint. For Q2 2024, we have three big requests: automated data import from ERP systems (requested by 18 of our 150 customers), a dashboard builder for custom reports (requested by 12 customers), and multi-language report generation (requested by 6 customers but including our largest account worth $120K annually). We can probably deliver two of these if we stretch, but not all three. My assumption is that the ERP integration will unlock the most growth because it reduces manual data entry, which our churn survey shows is the top frustration for 40% of departing customers. But I'm uncertain whether losing our largest account's feature request would cost us more revenue than the ERP integration would gain. I need a recommendation on what we should not build next quarter, for me to present to our leadership team at Q2 planning on April 1.
